commenti.body:
Here's my reading,
I think it's important to remember that Barbie and Ken belong to a fantasy world called Barbieland. Ken's world centering around Barbie is all he knows by design. 

What is Barbieland for? It's a fantasy world without contradiction. It functions to help women cope with patriarchy and smooth over cracks/contradictions in the real social relations for women under capitalism. 

Ken is some ideal form of a man as he is imagined in a supposedly good world where women have power. Barbie is also an idealized vision of the woman who can have any job, ie full participation in capitalism. They are non-sexed because this fantasy is about capitalism and selling women the idea of working. It's not really about following your desire but accepting the ones given to you. 

Of course this fantasy begins to crack because it doesn't function anymore. Daughter sees through it and mom is depressed. 

When men try to conform to what they think women want they end up thinking like Ken. But Barbieland isn't a place of liberation; it's really just a sort of sad inversion where women get to imagine themselves as the ones running the show, without a fundamental structural difference from the way patriarchy functions irl. Is this what women want? Is this what men should want if they are feminists? No, these are desires being sold to us. 

 If we understand patriarchy as men getting what they want at the expense of women we won't be able to imagine past this simple reversal. I think the movie is arguing that patriarchy is *neither* men *nor* women getting what they want (at the expense of women). Remember when Ken was talking about patriarchy and said something like "yeah I kinda lost interest when I realized it wasn't so much about horses". 

The way out, the movie is saying, is recognizing your own, more authentic or singular (unique to you) desire that was not simply given to you by social fantasies of how to be. 

By the end of the movie, Barbieland of course can't change that much because the real world didn't, but our main characters realized that they exceed their socially given identities. Or rather, they realize they don't have to live up to/conform to the ideal types they started the movie as. We're all Kenough.

Barbie is sexed by the end because she went from being a fantasy object of capitalism to being a real contradictory woman. 

I think the movie is very messy and somewhat symptomatic of the social contradictions it was trying to discern,  especially as it comes to what it almost but doesn't exactly critique about capitalism. But this fantasy world buttressing the real world, showing how the real world is based on fantasy itself, for me is the central key for deciphering the movie.

I do find that there's a lot of pressure on men to "become Men", that is, our status is something we must earn rather than something we already are, and a big part of that is acquiring (emphasis on this word!) a woman. You are less of a Man if you can't or won't. I don't know personally if women also share this pressure, but I certainly feel it.

To achive Maleness, you must pass through a series of trials (which aren't always possible) and when you fail, you are expected to suffer and feel guilt, because rather than an event that didn't come to you, you're told it's YOUR fault that YOU didn't succeed.

>but what if part of who he is includes wanting to have a Barbie by his side?

It shouldn't. That's the problem. Wanting her should be a side project disconnected from his identity. All successes and failures should. This has only become more obvious nowadays because the trials are harder to pass now (buying a house with a yard and a dog? Impossible), but it was always true.

>I feel like a desire for love is natural, normal, and maybe inevitable.

I agree, but tying your identity to your desires and to external validation is inevitably going to lead to suffering if/when you fail to satisfy them. Defining Masculinity as being able to do X is poisonous for that reason.

Side note: I find it interesting that Ken's plight was already cooking, and Barbie only gave him the tools to start the revolution. If she hadn't been played with by the mom, Ken would still be feeling rejected, and would have done something else. He was always the main crisis.

Hmmm. So I’m a woman and aroace. Honestly it hadn’t even occurred to me that Barbie’s rejection of Ken might be a “nod” to aroaces. since I read it more as Barbie not being interested in Ken specifically (many people can relate to the experience of someone liking you who you don’t like back, and vice versa) and going through a “taking some me time” period to figure out who she is outside of Barbieland before she looks for love/a relationship. Honestly, maybe easy for me to say since I’m not interested in relationships, but I think that that’s a very important thing for people to do in the early adulthood in general (unless you end up with your high school/college sweetheart) since I’ve seen many friends who go from relationship to relationship and seemingly don’t really know themselves outside of a relationship. So, as a single, professional thirtysomething woman that aspect of the movie spoke to me without my sexual/romantic orientation even coming into it. (As an aside, I felt very similarly about Jo’s storyline in the 2019 Little Women, which I re-watched recently.)

More to your general point, though, the most interesting thing about Barbie, to me, is that the female empowerment stuff fell relatively flat and felt trite and maybe even outdated to some people (2016-Clinton-campaign feminism is how I heard some people describe it) but the Ken stuff is what really touched a nerve, especially for men. Anecdotally, I’ve seen a lot of joking but also serious “he’s just like me fr” reactions both from my guy friends and online. I think the Ken stuff is what makes the movie a little bit quietly revolutionary and shines a light on something people have been feeling but haven’t had the words or felt comfortable articulating for a long time, i.e. that The Patriarchy (tm) harms not just women but men too and that the project of feminism is about breaking down those patriarchal systems to everyone’s benefit. I don’t necessarily think this movie is perfect in its portrayal of that stuff (as your post demonstrates, OP) but it’s importance lies in the fact that it has opened the door to these conversations on a much wider, more mainstream scale.

I think that there's a difference between tying your masculinity to romance, and also trying to find and build a committed relationship that will become a part of your identity.

IE being a man is not dependent on anything but being an adult human male (IDK if this is controversial to say or not but I think gender distinctions no longer seem meaningful to me, the only thing that seems to matter is bio sex for health reasons and gender presentation for aesthetic reasons). But also part of the way specific men want to specifically embody their masculinity may include a committed partner who will become a significant part of their identity. I see no reason to believe that this is an unhealthy behavior, you will be let down and disappointed by this partner, perhaps even left, but that is part of the drama that makes life interesting and meaningful. Attempting to disentangle your identity from dependence on others makes life less colorful and less interesting, frankly.

Yes, the desire itself is crucial and healthy. The problem is how you go about it. 

Imagine punishing yourself for not having qualified to the sportsball tournament you so desperately wanted to attend. "It's in my blood! I was born to be a sportsball athlete!" Anyone would tell you it's good to have goals, but nobody was born to be anything, and you're not less for not achieving this. 

A healthy approach would be putting in the work, hoping for the best, but accepting defeat if it did arrive. It's the self-punishment part that I have an issue with. You have two defeated people, but one of them finds their very existence put into question by something they didn't have control over (the tournament, Barbie not wanting a relationship), and the other one managing the pain and trying to heal and move on.

Ken is not a real man. He’s a stand in for some real issues but he’s not motivated like a real man. He is a child’s toy that mainly is designed to idolize Barbie. He serves no real other purpose. As a result his journey goes from, trying to get Barbie’s attention, to manipulating the Barbie world to get Barbie’s attention and then realizing he no longer needs her attention. 

They don’t “fall in love” because neither of them really loved each other. They were just doing whatever they were programmed to do. They have to first grow as characters to become human in some way before they could ever really experience love and deep connection with another human. That is the transition from toy to human. The movie doesn’t dismiss romantic love. It holds it in such high regard as to say the only way that can really exist is between to real people. Not shallow emulations of people.

I took kens lesson as. You don’t have to define yourself through your job. He can be more than beach you can be more than whatever your job. You don’t have to define yourself by the rigidity of whatever masculinity is seen as at the time. The relationship your in also does not have to be the end all be all.

To me Ken was different characters in different scenes. Initially when we me Ken it almost seemed like he was in some sort of Groundhog Day horror movie - doomed to repeat the same meaningless actions over and over because he has no autonomy.

In the second act where he reads a book on patriarchy theory and decides 'this is the good stuff' (something nobody has ever thought) he is a totally different character, and abruptly lurches from having absolutely no agency over anything in his life to completely upending Barbie society effortlessly and instantly. I mean, I get that he's doing this as a contrived plot point so the Barbies can overcome adversity and 'win'. But it doesn't seem like any sort of logical character progression.

And then he turns out not to be the comic book villain after all.

I think you’re taking the movie a little too literally as a specific societal commentary. Sure, it has social commentary, but the overall message is much simpler and more universal.

The bigger idea is everyone is flawed. The creator of Barbie, the execs, the Barbie’s, and the kens. They are all in some way defined by their role.

The execs want to make money, so their motivation for doing ‘good’ is always flawed. The Ken’s and Barbie’s are bound by the rules of barbieland, and so they are run into trouble even when trying to do good.

In every scenario, it’s about well intentioned people doing bad things without realizing it.

The parts you mention about the Ken’s are just because of who they are. They literally have no genitals and in barbieland, no one has sex or falls in love. They’re dolls designed to be purchased individually, which unintentionally leads them all to being selfish and self absorbed to some degree, because a single doll is marketed as a single product for a child to play with. 

IMO the Ken’s are really a mixture of men and women - they are oppressed by the flipped gender roles of barbieland where women oppress men, but the Ken’s also rebel in ways real men can rebel by holding on to toxic behavior. But they are doing so in response to toxic behavior the Barbie’s exhibit of oppressing the men and shunning the disfigured Barbie. Just no one realizes they are being shitty, which is more the point imo - lots of good people doing crappy things even with good intentions.

There is a huge difference between wanting romantic love and wanting romantic love from a specific person. The problem with Ken is not that he wanted love, it’s that he was making Barbie his entire identity. And just because Barbie is not shown to be interested in romance during the movie, that doesn’t mean that the movie is saying that women shouldn’t be interested in romance. It’s just saying that Barbie specifically does not have romantic feelings at this point in time.

fucking terrible flick. too "obvious", too preachy, too cringey, with bad performances all around. sorry but i simply do not find margot robbie a good actress, all i can see and hear is naomi from the wolf of wall street. ryan gosling needs to work on his voice and basic intonation. will ferrell is still a doofus who believes LOUD = FUNNY, matter fact the entire mattel board subplot was catastrophic, deduced to cheap slapstick """comedy""". this might be a male inside me speaking, but i just found the film too mean spirited and rather cheap.

Barbie isn't that much of a feminist film, I'm just aghast at the people who take this movie so seriously. I liked Greta Gerwig better when she wasn't in league with Mattel and was still playing the hot tomboy friend in House of the Devil or making annoying mumblecore films like Frances Ha. 

Barbie is actually pretty right-wing in content. You probably shouldn't spend so much time "chewing" it.

Well real academic feminists and leftists don't care for the whole Mattel angle and the cheap "white feminism" marketed there-in, so I doubt it's "the male in you."

Margot Robbie has started to get on my nerves too. I think she's received peak facial exposure. I hope this mean she'll go away soon.
